subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRY INTO PARLIAMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRY INTO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to avail myself of the privilege, which is afforded at this time, of congratulating the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the tenth anniversary of his entry into the House of Commons. Each one of those of us who believe in our particular form of democratic government shares the hope that men who have attained success in their own particular field of activity, whatever it may be, will show the same willingness to serve the public that has been shown by the Prime Minister of Canada. It was to serve his country that he gave up the comfortable security of his own home and, may I add, the assured income of a leader of the bar. Those who do not belong to his own party will, I am sure, pay tribute to the spirit of public service which prompted his entry into this house just as much as those who are associated with him in his own party.
I am particularly pleased that we are afforded the opportunity to pay him our respects in this way, because I am inclined to think that never was there a time when it was so desirable that the thought be impressed upon the mind of every Canadian, particularly young Canadians, that the vigour and surviving strength of our democratic system depends on the willingness of those who are able to do their own job well to enter the parliament of Canada and give the advantage of their experience to the deliberations of this house. Whether it may be in public or in private life, I trust and I am confident that the Prime Minister will at all times have in his heart a feeling of satisfaction in knowing that, whatever our political opinions may be, we all respect him for the public service he has rendered.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRY INTO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
This group would like to associate itself, Mr. Speaker, with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has said concerning the service of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to his country and this parliament.
It is not often that we find ourselves in such complete agreement with the leader of the opposition as we do on this occasion. Speaking for myself, I can say that I have particularly enjoyed-I think that is the word I should use-the almost unfailing courtesy of the Prime Minister in dealing with the matters that come up in this house. I say "almost" because there are perhaps moments that would try the temper of any person; but he seldom allows himself the pleasure of replying in kind. I think that those of us who have been here for some time all appreciate the parliamentary courtesies that he has shown us. I want to wish him success and long life to carry on the duties that he has taken up at a critical time in Canada's history.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRY INTO PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we all appreciate this opportunity of joining in an expression of good will and congratulations to the Prime Minister. After ten years in parliament one can truthfully say that he has certainly maintained and retained a sense of fairness and a sense of balance. One often wonders just how he has been able to keep his sense of proportion in view of all the things with which he has to contend. I know that sometimes we are inclined to try to rulb the Prime Minister a little bit in order to get a certain reaction from him. If we do so occasionally, it is only because we love him. I think that it is a sincere statement on the part of anyone who cares to speak in this house, when he says that we all greatly appreciate the fine qualities of the Prime Minister. We all join in telling him this. If we have a little bit of fun once in a while out of his reactions, it is certainly only because of-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRY INTO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to find words to express adequately my appreciation

Congratulations to Prime Minister of what has been said here this afternoon and, over and above that, my appreciation of the sentiments that have prompted the kind remarks that you have just heard. They are compensation for whatever one can do in the attempt to be of service to his fellow citizens and to carry out his part in this undertaking in which we are all engaged, namely that of making our democracy effective and worth while for all Canadian citizens. I appreciate, even more than the expressions that were used this afternoon, the constant friendship that I have felt from every member of this house during a period of almost ten years now that it has been my privilege to sit here. I think the leader of the opposition has uttered a truth that we ourselves should not forget and that we should not allow our fellow citizens to forget, namely that each one of us who feels that this system of social organization is the best that human ingenuity has been able to devise for the administration of the common interests of free men and women in organized society must also feel that each one of us should be at the disposal of his fellow citizens for any responsibility they wish at any time to entrust him with. I am sure that this is as true of every other member of this House of Commons as I hope it is of me: our real compensation for any public service we perform is the satisfaction of knowing that we are doing something for the maintenance of that system for our own generation and for the generations that will follow us in this country which has such a glorious future before it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: PRIVILEGE, MR. LAPOINTE    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON NOVEMBER 30
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of
privilege, I should like to clarify certain information which I gave to the house on Friday last during the discussion of Bill No. 27, to amend the Pension Act, in the committee stage. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked if those veterans who had the right to treatment because they were receiving the unemployability supplement might not lose the right because the supplement was being replaced by an increase in the pension. My reply might have indicated that such veterans' treatment rights would be unchanged.
On further considering the question and reply in Hansard, I find that my answer might be construed as going beyond what I intended. I had in mind then what had been decided in regard to a certain group of those who received the unemployability supplement, namely those who had formerly been on war veterans allowance. It is certainly
[Mr. St Laurent.1
the intention that these veterans, though they went off war veterans allowance to receive the unemployability supplement and may now not be eligible for war veterans allowance by reason of the increase in pensions, will still be eligible for treatment.
It is intended to protect the eligibility for treatment of veterans in this group by a revision of the regulation which provides for free treatment for pensioners and veterans with service in a theatre of actual war who are unable to pay for the cost of their treatment. I believe it is done at the present time under regulation 5A. As hon. members know, an income ceiling is set in this regulation, and the veteran with an income below the ceiling is eligible for treatment. The ceiling was previously set so that the 100 per cent pensioner who had no other financial resources would be eligible. It will now be necessary to adjust the income ceiling to provide that this principle will apply when the new rates of pension are in effect after January 1.
In other words, those eligible for free treatment before the unemployability supplement was brought into effect will still be eligible for it after it has lapsed and in spite of the pension increases.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: AUTOMATIC VENDING MACHINES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. What legislation, if any, is the Department of Justice contemplating to prevent persons under sixteen years of age from buying cigarettes from automatic vending machines?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AUTOMATIC VENDING MACHINES
speechtext:
This is the type of question in reference to which I am very glad that my hon. friend gave me notice. We are not contemplating any change in the law because we are of the opinion that the law as it stands at the present time is sufficient for the purpose. It is contained in section 2 of the tobacco restraint act or, more fully "an act to restrain the use of tobacco by young persons". This section reads in part as follows:
2. Every one is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction . . . who. directly or indirectly, sells or gives or furnishes to a person under the age of sixteen years any cigarettes or cigarette papers, whether for his own use or not, or sells or gives or furnishes to such person tobacco in any form other than cigarettes which tobacco he knows or has reason to believe is for the use of that person.
We believe that that section, if enforced, is adequate for the purpose.

subtopic: AUTOMATIC VENDING MACHINES
speechtext: Since such sale can only be prevented by prohibiting the use of such machines, is the department contemplating such prohibition?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. Would he state whether the present rate of enlistments in the three branches of our armed services is adequate to supply replacements for our forces in Korea, and also to fill our commitments for additional troops in Europe to meet our obligations under the Atlantic pact agreements?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: RATE OF ENLISTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member gave notice of his question, but it was in slightly different form. I do not know what he means by "our commitments for additional troops in Europe to meet our obligations" under the North Atlantic pact. The only commitments we have made are those which have been reported to this parliament.
With regard to ground forces, we shall fulfil our agreement to have a brigade in Europe before the end of the year. We have no present intention of increasing this force.

We have in the replacement groups and schools sufficient men to meet all estimated wastage and replacements for a considerable time ahead. However, we want a continuous flow of recruits at an average rate somewhat in excess of what we are getting today.
In this connection the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said in a broadcast last night:
In building up the strength required to prevent aggression and ensure the peace, there is a duty for everyone. It is not something we can leave to the other fellow.
We need a steady flow of young men for the highest service of all-whether it be on the battlefields of Korea, on the ramparts of freedom in Europe, or in our own northland.

speechtext: On the orders' of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
subtopic: PROTEST AGAINST PREMATURE PAYMENT OF MORTGAGE MONEY UNDER NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked about loans under the National Housing Act to some forty residents of East Kildonan.
I have looked into the matter and I find that these owners made a complaint to the Winnipeg office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation about two weeks ago. Because the lending institution is the administrator of the mortgages, complaints of this kind are referred by Central Mortgage to the lending institution.
It appears that the dispute between the owners and the builders arises not on account of failure of the lending institution to retain a hold-back because of unfinished work, but rather dissatisfaction by the owners about the quality of work performed by the builder.
The hon. member refers to a protest against the payment of the balance of the mortgage moneys before receiving clearance from the buyers of these homes. At the time of the completion of the sale, each one of these purchasers signed a direction to the lending institution which reads:
The undersigned hereby declares that the said premises have been accepted from the vendor and irrevocably authorizes the company to pay the proceeds of the said additional loan to . . . the vendor of the property, upon registration of transfer of title to me.
Therefore, it would appear that the buyers were satisfied with the houses at the time of occupation and the complaints are, as I have already suggested, about work which, after occupation, is not satisfactory to the owners.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The hon. member asks what can be done to meet the claim of the purchasers of these homes. speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, December 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. 1606
The Address-Mr. Low Robert Cauchon for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Argue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment of the debate on Monday we were discussing the amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), which was in these terms:
That the following words be added to the address: "This house regrets, however, that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for the immediate payment to producers of 75 per cent of the initial price of farm stored grain."
I had just completed saying that it was our fond hope, under the circumstances, that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) might be inclined to pull a Pete Karpuk play, and rush out from the bench to the assistance of his teammates. We were very much disappointed. I went home that night sad at heart. The reason I was sad at heart was that I could not help thinking about what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) probably was doing. I knew that he must have gone home and spent many long sleepless hours saying over and over again to himself, "Oh, where is my wandering boy tonight?" The boy was wandering in more than one sense, I would judge, from what transpired during last week and the early part of this week.
I do not suppose that there is very much we can do about that particular part of the discussion until such time as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) returns to Ottawa and we find out exactly what is to be done. Let me say, however, that I support the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I do so because I think it is a good amendment; I think it is timely and I think the assistance it requests from the government is not only necessary but urgent.
All too often when such matters as those covered by this amendment are brought before the house some members will say, "Here is just one more unjustifiable beef on the part of the western farmers." I know that a good many hon. members are inclined to disregard appeals by western members made from time to time on behalf of their constituents. Perhaps their indifference arises from the fact that they lack firsthand information. They have no knowledge of the facts concerning the conditions under which western farmers are trying to carry on and to do their part in feeding the Canadian people as well as many people in other lands.
Let me point out that there are many things which the Canadian farmers cannot possibly (Mr. Martin.]

do for themselves, which only the government can accomplish. It is those things about which we speak so often in this house. I am quite sure that no one can say honestly that the farmers of Canada have been given too much help in times past. I doubt if anyone can bring facts to prove such a case. To me it is just as certain that it cannot be honestly said that the farmers have had even a fair deal. In my judgment, they have rarely had a fair deal. Until comparatively recent years the farmers in this country were looked upon as clodhopping work horses who should not grumble as long as body and soul were able to hang together. However, with the growth of farm organizations and commodity pools the situation became somewhat better and since that time governments have been inclined to listen more attentively to the farmers and their requests for justice.
Even with all that, the farmers still are not getting a fair deal as compared with the other component parts of Canada unlimited. I do not need to remind the house of some of the reasons why I make that statement. In the first place, let me name a few things to bring back to the minds of hon. members how the farmers of this country have suffered. At any time when our farmers have been called upon in emergencies they have responded nobly with an all-out effort. I think one of the finest examples of this was their response during the second world war, when, faced with a shortage of labour, with their sons in the army, navy and air force, they carried on and put forth a prodigious effort to produce the necessary foods and commodities so that we could make a real war effort.
In the second place, our farmers have always been prepared to make sacrifices in the national interest. No one can disprove that. Some of us object to the unnecessary and unequal sacrifices which they are often called upon to make. It is just that feeling that activates us in protesting against the inaction of the government with respect to advances on farm-stored grain.
In the third place, down through the years our farmers have been hounded by income tax sleuths under one of the most unfair enforcement programs I have ever heard of anywhere. They have been hounded into making admissions and doing things which have placed an unnecessary burden of taxation upon them. None of us mind paying fair taxes. We do not mind having to make these payments when they are fair and just, but some of the things that have been done in carrying out this enforcement program in western Canada would make you weep.

Farmers out there have been discouraged because of this. It is going to take a long time to regain their confidence.
In the fourth place, our farmers have borne the cost of subsidizing cheap bread for all the Canadian people over a fairly substantial number of years. At the same time they took a beating under the British wheat agreement. When it was finally decided by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the government that a partial compensation of $65 million should be made to the farmers we heard complaints all through the house of this "gift" that was being made.
I want to say just a word about some of the newspapers in this country which indicated in large headlines that the government had decided to make a gift of $65 million to the farmers. That was the most unfair insinuation that could possibly be made against a portion of our population which had risen so nobly to the occasion during the war and since. That $65 million was not a gift even in the most extreme view that anyone might take. It was nothing but partial compensation for the losses the farmers had suffered as a result of the subsidization program for cheap bread in Canada and for the beating they took under the British wheat agreement. It was nothing more than a token payment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The government did not pay it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is quite true; the government did not pay it, it came out of the taxation of all the people of Canada where it should have come from. Any program of subsidizing ought to be borne fairly and justly by all the people and not by just one-third of the population as was the case here.
The fifth important thing to remember is that as far as my memory goes the farmers have been forced to buy in a protected market the things that they require in order to be able to produce, and have been forced to sell in unprotected markets. As a consequence the farmers of this country have constantly been subjected to a beating under the Canadian tariff. Very little if anything has been done about it and they still must suffer.
The farmers were promised parity prices after the war as a reward for accepting lower than world prices for their wheat and wheat products during the war and afterwards. There is no sign of parity as yet although it is now six years since the war ended. We hope most sincerely that parity prices will come and we should all put forth our best efforts to achieve that result. I feel
The Address-Mr. Low that in no other way can fair treatment and justice be extended to the farmers of our country.
It seems to me that what is asked for in this statement is quite reasonable. There may be some hon. members who will feel that the 75 per cent asked for is hardly justified, and perhaps that is so. I cannot justify it entirely but I do think it is something to shoot at. But if the government should come forward with a program of advances of something less than 75 per cent of the initial payment, I do not imagine the farmers are going to kick too much, although 75 per cent may possibly be perfectly justified. Keeping in mind that the initial payment for wheat is only a portion of the final price, it seems to me that 75 per cent may not represent too high a percentage by way of advance. Certainly no one can put up a case that would in any way change our minds with respect to the need of some such advance being made.
Let me say a word about one other matter. About ten days ago the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) was asked if he would announce government policy with respect to the importation into Canada of commercial driers. I think it was understood that there were two types that would be involved. First there was the type that might be brought in by a small co-operative association of farmers as a co-operative enterprise to dry their own wheat. The other type was the kind that would probably be installed by commercial line or pool elevators for the purpose of drying wheat as it came into the elevators. The minister made an announcement as the result of which co-operatives or individuals will be allowed to bring in driers to do co-operative or commercial work, not completely free of duty but on the basis of paying for each month or part of a month that the drier remains in Canada one-sixtieth of the duty that normally would be paid. Under that policy the understanding was that the driers would only be in Canada on lease and would be returnable or exportable at the end of a certain period of time to the country from which they came.
I do not think that is sufficient. We are in an emergency year when there is a tremendous amount of grain that needs to be dried. The grain will spoil if it is not dried soon. If it is left until spring, with the advent of warm weather it is inevitable that a great many thousands and perhaps millions of bushels will never reach the mills in anything like millable condition. In such an emergency year I think the minister would be thoroughly justified in allowing

The Address-Mr. Bater a reasonable number of commercial driers, which would be installed by country elevators, to come into Canada duty free, not just on lease but on purchase. My own feeling is that nobody would criticize action of that kind. The grain has to be dried somewhere and the best place to dry it is where it is first received. Most of the line elevators just have not the drying facilities, and for that reason I think the minister should give careful consideration to allowing such driers to enter the country duty free.
To sum up our attitude, we bespeak for our Canadian farmers only those things that are fair and just. We do not want for them anything that is not fair and just. The farmers should be assured of a return for their efforts that will represent their fair share of the national income. I do not think we should go on year after year imposing conditions upon the country, or allowing conditions to continue, under which our farmers, although they represent perhaps 23 per cent of the population, to receive out of the national income not more than 10 per cent, and in some cases somewhat less than 10 per cent. That condition must not be allowed to continue. If it is, no one can say that justice is being done to Canadian farmers. I want it definitely known that my associates and I strongly support the amendment before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say that I support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), after having listened to the arguments presented by the various members who have spoken in this debate. I am one of those members who are not very well informed about the details of the wheat marketing situation, but I think members who have spoken in favour of the amendment have given valid reasons for the government taking such action. I also think that, according to reports we have read in the press of the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the amendment is not far out of line with government policy.
When the hon. member for Assiniboia was speaking the other evening I am sure a good many members were interested in the figures he presented dealing with the income tax collected from farmers in various provinces of Canada. I am sure many of us were much concerned with the apparent disparity in the amounts of tax collected. I am one of a goodly number of members in the house who look forward with some interest to an explanation of those figures on the part of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). I am not going to say any more on that point at this time because sometimes explanations can be given for bare figures that present a somewhat different picture.

The amendment largely has to do with something that concerns the life of the body. I am going to take the opportunity presented by this debate to deal with something that I consider concerns the life of the spirit, and a good many other persons in Canada are of the same opinion. I want to speak for a few minutes on a matter that is of great concern to many of my constituents and other Canadians at this time. It is a matter that is of great concern to the members of this group. I refer to the mystery surrounding the possible release of the former nazi general, Kurt Meyer.
I am anxious to express the anxiety of this group because we know a large number of Canadians are concerned about this question. All members of the group for whom I am speaking have received resolutions from trade unions, Canadian Legion branches, women's organizations, and also quite a number of letters. In addition, the press generally throughout Canada has shown in various editorials considerable concern, and with respect to my own constituency editorials in the press have expressed similar concern. In this, the press is reflecting the concern and opinion of a large number of Canadian people. I was interested to receive only yesterday a letter from a Canadian of French descent in my constituency who is over 75 years of age, a man on whose logging sleds I used to ride as a boy forty-five years ago. He writes quite a touching letter to me. He cannot understand why, if this man has been sentenced as a war criminal and in view of what has been suffered by Canadian's as a result of his actions, there is a possibility of his being released.
It is because of that concern that I feel justified in taking a few minutes to deal with this very important matter. I must explain before proceeding that it is not a question of a vindictive attitude toward a person or an enemy. This is a matter that concerns the Canadian people from the point of view of justice, the principles we have declared from time to time in this house and throughout the country, and from the point of view of national policy. It is on that basis I wish to make some representations this afternoon. The concern of the Canadian people has been considerably increased as a result of the newspaper account written by Mr. Douglas How, Canadian Press correspondent, dealing with the fact that Kurt Meyer had been given several days holiday from prison in Germany. In view of the concern of the Canadian public as a whole, I think parliament and the people of Canada are entitled to a frank and complete statement from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton)
The Address-Mr. Herridge before this session ends. Only something of that nature can allay the fears of many persons throughout the country.
In order to bring the picture into focus within the compass of one very short speech, I want to review briefly the developments in connection with this matter. I find that the question was first raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the external affairs committee of 1946. At that time he brought to the attention of the committee the fact that the War Measures Act had expired, and that it was quite possible that the release of Kurt Meyer could be obtained because he was formally held under the terms of that act. I judge from a reading of that evidence, and a reading of Hansard of a slightly later date, that it was because of the alertness of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that shortly afterwards the government introduced the War Crimes Act.
I am going to read briefly from the debate in connection with that act. At page 4382 of Hansard for 1946 the hon. member for Lake Centre had this to say in dealing with the question:
In other words, while now the minister takes the view that these regulations were drafted as part and parcel of international law, or under the powers of His Majesty under royal warrant, the regulations provided that they were drafted entirely under the War Measures Act with the result-at least so I contended-that in view of the fact that penalties under the War Measures Act were restricted to five years or a fine of $2,000, no statute could grant to a subsidiary measure by way of order in council passed thereunder the power to impose a heavier penalty. Among others, Kurt Meyer, a prisoner in Dorchester penitentiary, might have made an application to the courts for the purpose of determining that his imprisonment was illegal and, as a result, the doors of that penitentiary might have been opened, should the court find that an illegal sentence, beyond that provided for under the War Measures Act, had been imposed.
While the minister has said there was an opinion from the Department of Justice that such a possibility was not a probability, I would point out that in giving evidence on the matter before the committee on external affairs the deputy minister of justice said he had no doubt that a forceful argument could be made in support of the contention that I advanced to the contrary.
So I presume, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians generally have to thank the alertness of the hon. member for Lake Centre for the fact that Kurt Meyer is not free today.
Proceeding with a short review of this case, I find that I raised the question on March 2 of this year during a debate on the Defence Production Act, as a result of receiving a number of representations from individuals, trade unions and the Legion. I did not get very far, as I was ruled out of order. I was able to express my views only briefly. Then on October 19 the question of Meyer's release was raised by the hon. member for Lake

The Address-Mr. Decore parliament what are the regulations in. this British prison as to treatment of inmates. When the government does this, it might answer the question it has so long evaded:	Does it intend to release
Meyer?
Until this question is answered, many Canadians will continue to fear that a commander of SS troops found responsible for the murder of Canadian prisoners is to be given his freedom. That such a man should be set free to serve in NATO forces is an intolerable proposition to almost everyone except the communists, who would he handed a choice piece of anti-democratic propaganda.
The government can settle this uncertainty quite easily. All that is required is a statement that under no circumstances will Meyer be released.
The release of Kurt Meyer for use in a future German army is, I am sure, in the opinion of the majority of thh Canadian people completely morally indefensible. On that basis, if Hitler were alive we could seek his support as an ally in the defence of freedom. Just let us realize, Mr. Speaker, that if this man were released and assumed command of a German division, under the terms of military law Canadian troops serving in Germany would be required to salute this German war criminal when passing him on the street. I am sure there are a great number of Canadians who do not view that situation with any relish.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the circumstances and in view of the concern felt by the Canadian people, the release of Kurt Meyer would be an offence against the memory of our gallant dead. It would be an offence and an outrage against their sorrowing next of kin. It would show a complete lack of consideration of the efforts made and the fighting done by the veterans of this country in two great wars. It would mean the complete disregard of the opinion of the great majority of the Canadian people. His release would be a violation of our declared democratic principles and practices. As a policy it would have, psychologically, most unfortunate effects. It would affect the morale of the Canadian people. It would affect their confidence and faith in our democratic cause. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker-and I speak with some heat on this question-in the long run democracy and freedom can only be satisfactorily defended by people who believe in freedom. Public concern demands from the minister before this session ends a complete and frank statement concerning this whole question. Only that will allay the fears of the Canadian people at this time.
In conclusion I say that if we have faith in freedom's truth, let us prove it by our acts.

When the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke to the wheat pool, he was speaking on behalf of the Liberal candidate in Calgary West, make no mistake about that. It was for that reason that he made some reference to the western farmer.. Might I speak to this particular subamendment, Mr. Speaker. Let me read the wording of it:
That all the words in the amendment after the word "regrets" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"the serious difficulties encountered by the western farmers in harvesting their crops,-
No one could have any objection to that part of the amendment and I certainly could support it. Then the. amendment continues: -and commends Your Excellency's advisers for the continuing attention they have given to the problems caused thereby,-
With that part of the amendment I cannot agree, because the government has not been giving continuing attention to the problems. If they have, they have been on the outside looking through the farm window at the plight of the farmer who is on the inside. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) said, they are giving the farmer plenty of sympathy; but he cannot live on sympathy. His Excellency's advisers continue to stay on the outside and look in at the farmer's plight. The amendment might just as well read that way; it commends Your Excellency's advisers for standing on the outside and sympathizing with the farmer on the inside.
Then the amendment continues:
-and is confident that effective measures will continue-
How can something continue if it does not exist? The effective measures do not exist, and that is why the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) put his amendment. He wants some effective measures to be adopted; we all want effective measures to be adopted.

How can we vote for the continuance of something that does not exist? When the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) spoke to this subamendment they failed to tell the house of a single effective measure that exists today. You cannot find it in their speeches.
I close on that particular point and suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot see how anyone with any perception and appreciation of amendments can vote for an amendment like this one. The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking), who spoke a little while ago, said that this amendment was designed to split the farmers into groups. Nothing of the kind. What it may do-and I do not suppose it is designed to do it-is split the members of parliament from the west Into groups, but that is another thing altogether. It does not split the farmers into groups, for there is not a farmer in the country who would not vote for the amendment offered by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The fact of the matter is that every member of parliament would be required to vote as to whether or not he wants the farmers of the west to receive an advance payment on their stored grain. In order to avoid that necessity, my hon. friends of course come forward with a nebulous and meaningless subamendment. So far as we who come from western Canada are concerned, we are not going to vote for anything as nebulous as this subamendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to deal briefly with an inference which was raised by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Hetland) when he spoke with regard to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia. He indicated that if the amendment passed, any moneys advanced by the government for grain stored on the farm would become a charge against wheat board accounts, and any losses therefrom would be borne by the wheat growers as a whole. That inference cannot be drawn from the amendment at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not say that. I said that expenses in connection with inspection would be charged to the wheat board.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I will accept the hon. member's statement that he referred to expenses with regard to inspection. The amendment does not state that at all. The amendment asks His Excellency's advisers to give consideration to making an advance of 75 per cent of the value of farm stored grain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It does not go far enough. How about the man with grain in the swath?
The Address-Mr. Wright

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It states nothing about who shall take care of the expenses incurred in doing that; and it certainly was not the intention of -the mover of this amendment that those expenses should be charged against the farmers through the wheat board. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) comes back to this house, I hope any legislation he may present to take care of the serious situation which exists in the west will not be along that line, and that it will not make provision for an advance to the farmers on wheat that has not been threshed or that is under the snow in western Canada, which advance will be made by the wheat board, and that any losses which may be incurred as a result of that advance be a charge against the wheat board. If that is the type of legislation he intends to introduce I can assure the government that it will be opposed by those of us on this side of the house.
I know the hon. member for The Battle-fords (Mr. Bater) quite well. He is a practical farmer. When he introduced this subamendment I am sure he would have much preferred to introduce one which would add something to the amendment rather than one which merely expresses a pious hope. I am afraid he was in the unfortunate position where he could not offer any subamendment which would be an addition. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has not yet returned. Until he does, and until he informs the government what the government's policy is going to be with regard to any further advances, the government members find themselves in the position that they cannot offer anything in the way of substantial help to the farmers in western Canada. Apparently this is a one-man government.
We did not bring in this amendment with the idea that it met all the problems this year in western Canada. We introduced this amendment for one purpose, namely to get provision made for an advance on farm stored grain. That is something we in western Canada have been asking for, and which farm organizations have been asking for many years. A vote for the subamendment is a vote against the policy the farmers of western Canada have been asking for over a number of years now. That is the effect of it. It is voting for some pious hope rather than voting for something concrete, something we have been asking for over a number of years, which is quite another matter. When the amendment was introduced I stated that I thought it was good but that to meet the situation which existed this year some additional assistance was necessary. I

The Address-Mr. Wright recognized the fact that some additional assistance was necessary. Because the Minister of Trade and Commerce had indicated that the government were considering something in the way of further assistance, we did not extend our amendment. As reported at page 1546 of Hansard I stated:
I hope the government will give serious consideration to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia. As I said before, I do not think it goes far enough to meet the needs of all sections of the west at this time, but it is a step in the right direction. It is a good piece of permanent legislation which we should have on our statute books.
That is all we were offering, a sound amendment which would instruct the government to place on our statute books legislation which would make it possible for an advance to be made to farmers on grain stored on the farm. I hope western members will oppose the subamendment offered by the hon. member for The Battlefords because, in voting for it, they are voting against the best interests of the farmers in western Canada; they are voting against something for which the farmers in western Canada have been asking consistently over the last number of years, namely an advance on farm stored grain.

I was pointing out that no Canadian worthy of the name would object to paying a fair share of the taxes necessary to run this country, but that what Canadians are objecting to today is that there is to be no baby budget and no reduction of taxation at this session of parliament. The cost of living continues to rise; the latest available index indicates a further increase in the cost of living, induced in part by the fact that in his estimate last April the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made one of the most serious errors ever made in the history of this country.
As a consequence of that guess extra taxation was imposed. We in His Majesty's loyal opposition pointed out that such extra taxation was unnecessary in order to meet the costs of defence and the ordinary costs of government; but the government, with its all-powerful majority, brought in new taxes and increased the sales tax by 25 per cent and the income tax by 20 per cent over and above what had been paid in 1950. The Canadian people have been taken in to the extent of $604 million in the last seven months, or $45 per head.
